video:video.video:title: Why Your Poodle Has That Haircut (It's Hunting Gear, Not Fashion)
video:video.video:description: That Poodle haircut was never designed for a show ring. It was designed by duck hunters. The Poodle was a German duck dog first, and the clip kept his joints and organs warm in cold water. The pom poms are life jackets. Does yours lose his mind near water? Yes or no in the comments. Source: American Kennel Club, Poodle breed history.

video:video.video:title: The French Bulldog Was Bred for One Job. You're Sitting On It.
video:video.video:description: Your French Bulldog sitting on your lap is not just seeking comfort; it is the specific job this breed was created to do. French Bulldogs were originally bred by Nottingham lacemakers to serve as dedicated lap dogs. Unlike herding or guardian breeds built for farm work, these dogs were selected for their small size and companionship. With a maximum lap weight of 28 pounds, they are physically designed to curl up and settle in, making their desire to climb onto you when you sit down a direct result of their history rather than a behavioral issue. Understanding these breed traits helps explain why your Frenchie is so persistent about being close to you. He is not being clingy or needy; he is simply exhibiting the natural tendencies he was bred for centuries ago. By recognizing that his lap-sitting is a working behavior, you can better appreciate the specific history behind his personality.

video:video.video:title: Why Your Australian Shepherd Herds the Kids (It's Not Play)
video:video.video:description: Your Australian Shepherd circles the kids, nudges knees and nips heels because the AKC breed description calls it "an irresistible impulse to herd anything" — eye, stalk, chase, the hunting sequence with the ending bred out. And he isn't from Australia: the breed was developed on ranches in the American West. Your Australian Shepherd is not being aggressive; he is simply doing the job he was bred for. That intense focus is his work. This footage captures the natural herding instincts that define the breed. From the focused gaze to the specific stalking behavior, every movement is an ingrained sequence designed for controlling livestock. When your dog attempts to herd children or other family members, he is not misbehaving—he is exhibiting the classic traits of a herding breed. Understanding these ancient drives is the first step in managing your dog behavior at home. He is not broken; he is just working.

video:video.video:title: Why Your Doberman Won't Leave Your Side (It's Not Neediness)
video:video.video:description: Why does your Doberman lean on you and follow you from room to room? In the late 1800s a German tax collector named Louis Dobermann bred a dog to stay glued to one person on dangerous rounds — the "velcro Doberman" is over a century of selection, not neediness. On the American Temperament Test the Doberman passes 80% of the time (1,870 dogs tested). Sources: AKC Doberman Pinscher breed history · American Temperament Test Society breed statistics

video:video.video:title: Why Your Rottweiler Leans On You (It's Not Dominance)
video:video.video:description: Why does your Rottweiler lean on you? It's not dominance — the Rottweiler descends from Roman drover dogs and the butchers' dogs of Rottweil, Germany, bred to move cattle by leaning into them and to guard the money purse on the walk home. The lean is the job, two thousand years later. On the American Temperament Test the Rottweiler passes 85% of the time; the Golden Retriever, 86%. He's not broken. He's bred that way. video:video.video:description: A 2013 study in Tokyo found dogs catch yawns from humans — real yawns far more than fake ones, and most reliably from their own owner. Contagious yawning is an empathy marker; human children don't show it until around age four.
